When cancer comes to school

Supporting students affected by cancer.

Childhood cancer turns life upside down for everyone involved. Schools play an important role in the lives of students with cancer, offering them structure, friends, and a sense of normality. But this role doesn’t come with instructions. There’s no standard plan, because every family is different. As a teacher, it’s normal to feel lost about how to support your student. This guide helps you navigate it with more confidence, so that your student, their family, classmates and you feel cared for throughout. You don’t have to manage this alone.

Childhood cancer turns life upside down for everyone involved. Familiar routines are disrupted by hospital visits and uncertainty. For the ill student, this often means losing control over their daily life, while family members enter an emotional and organisational rollercoaster.

While the student’s health comes first, staying connected to school is vital for their wellbeing and sense of continuity. Schools also remain responsible for their student’s education throughout treatment. For those unfamiliar with childhood cancer, this can feel daunting. There is no one-size-fits-all support plan, as every case is different. Families vary greatly in their needs, treatment journeys, and comfort levels in talking about cancer. Some welcome openness and community support; others prefer to deal with cancer more privately. Some students can keep attending school with small adjustments, while others need major adaptations.

Supporting a student with cancer therefore calls for a personalised approach and consistent coordination with the family. It often involves understanding the impact of cancer and its treatment, communicating clearly, supporting classmates, asking consent about what can be shared, and remaining flexible and understanding throughout. It also means working closely with experienced partners such as the hospital school, whose guidance can help reduce pressure on both the school and the family.

This schoolkit shares tips, voices, and experiences from children with cancer, during and after treatment, along with their siblings, parents, and teachers. It aims to help schools understand what matters most to a family facing cancer. The first part is designed to help school teams support students affected by cancer. The second part is a practical toolkit for teachers on how to talk about cancer in class. In the annexes, you will find quick checklists for handling common issues, age-appropriate ideas for staying in touch and welcoming the student back, a sample letter to inform parents, a glossary to support classroom conversations, and further educational resources.

We hope this Schoolkit will help you navigate the complexities of having a child with cancer in your class with greater confidence, so that your student, their parents, classmates, and you feel cared for throughout the journey. It is designed to complement, not replace, human support and professional training, which will make the biggest difference.

Additional resources: resources.kickcancer.org/schoolkit

It reassured us that our child’s regular school remained ‘their school’. That sense of belonging was important, even when they couldn’t be there in person.

Celine – mother

Situation 01

Help! My student has cancer. What now?

Communication and coordination with the family, both during the student’s absence and after their return to school, are essential for providing appropriate support. How can schools approach this? What are the first steps, and what comes next?

Checklist

First steps

  • Agree with the school team who will contact the parents, for example the principal, the class teacher or the student support coordinator.
  • Has the family already contacted the school? Let them know you are thinking of them and ready to help. If not, the person you agreed on can make the first contact.
  • Arrange a first meeting with the parents to understand the situation, discuss how they would like to communicate and find out what support they need, including for any siblings at the school. Respect their privacy and follow their lead.
  • During that meeting, appoint a central coordinator together with the family as the key contact.
Annex 1 › Checklists › First steps

First things first

We weren’t ready to tell anyone. We needed time to process it ourselves.

Stephanie – mother
  • Parents under pressure. A cancer diagnosis is overwhelming. In the early stages especially, parents have so much to manage that communication can be difficult. They may not inform the school straight away, as they focus on treatment decisions and adjusting to their new reality.
  • Privacy and confidentiality. Parents are generally not legally required to share the diagnosis with the school. If they wish to keep it private or to limit information, this needs to be respected unless clear health and safety concerns arise. Parental consent is always required before sharing any medical information with school staff or classmates.
  • Benefits of openness. In most cases, openness is preferable. Informing key staff enables more personalised support, while honest conversations with classmates can reduce confusion, anxiety and rumours – especially when treatment causes visible changes.
Part 1 › 3. Communication and coordination › First things first

Central coordinator

It meant a lot when one staff member became our main contact. We didn’t have to repeat everything ten times.

Evelien – mother

When a student has cancer, one of the first helpful steps is to appoint a school-wide key contact person. Their role is to coordinate support and communication between the school team, the student and their parents, siblings, classmates, and external partners such as the hospital school. By centralising information and follow-up, this person can help reduce the load on both parents and teachers. A central coordinator is often invaluable, especially in secondary schools where more teachers are involved, both during the student’s absence and after they return to school.

Part 1 › 3. Communication and coordination › Central coordinator

Starting the conversation

Once the family is ready to share information, they often appreciate being invited to an initial meeting with three main purposes:

  • Understanding the situation. The family can provide basic information about the diagnosis, treatment, and how long the student may be away from school.
  • Communication preferences. Together, you can explore what to share, when, with whom and how – with the family always deciding what feels right. You can differentiate between more sensitive information for a restricted circle and more general information for wider awareness. You can also agree on a central coordinator, discuss how the student prefers to stay in touch with classmates, where classmates can go with their questions, and when to inform siblings’ classmates. Cultural beliefs may also shape how families view and talk about cancer – for example concerns about stigma or misconceptions that cancer is ‘contagious’ or the parents’ fault – and this may influence what they choose to share.
  • Support needs. Many parents say it helps to know that the school is there to help, while also recognising that families differ in how much involvement they want. It may be too early at this point, but together you can explore flexible learning options – school, home, hospital, or online – and, where available, ask the hospital school and support services to help design a personalised educational care plan . With parental consent, hospital pedagogical staff or their team’s psychologist can also brief teachers or classmates. Siblings may also need dedicated support. The Centre for Student Guidance (CLB) or Centre Psycho-Médico-Social (CPMS) may also be able to help.
Part 1 › 3. Communication and coordination › Starting the conversation

Follow-up

For families, it can be reassuring to know that communication is not left to chance. Planned conversations help ensure that support is timely and that changing needs are noticed early. A meeting provides an opportunity to pause, share updates, and adjust together what is needed at home, at school, or in contact with classmates. Consider meeting to:

  • Develop a personalised educational care plan
  • Discuss what to share with classmates and their parents
  • Explore ways classmates can stay connected during longer absences
  • Prepare for the student’s return during or after treatment
  • Consider the needs of siblings
Part 1 › 3. Communication and coordination › Follow-up

Where to go next

Situation 02

How to stay involved during treatment?

When a student is away for treatment, the aim is to keep them connected to school while learning continues in other ways. This part covers who does what, how a personalised educational care plan works, the options for learning from a distance, and simple ways to keep the class in touch.

Checklist
  • Coordinate with the family, ideally via the central coordinator.
  • Keep the student formally registered, share updates with the hospital school, and plan for a gradual return.
  • Follow a personalised educational care plan which sets priorities, expectations, and a realistic mix of learning options.
  • Use distance-learning options during treatment.
  • Keep the social connection with classmates alive.
  • Watch for sibling dynamics. If a brother or sister feels uncomfortable at school, check in, normalise their feelings, and consider flexible expectations.
Annex 1 › Checklists › How to stay involved during treatment?

Developing a plan

During treatment, I kept worrying I’d fall behind – maybe even have to repeat a year – and be separated from my friends. It felt like cancer wasn’t just taking away my health, but also my chance to stay on the same path as everyone else my age.

Anke – student

A personalised educational care plan can reassure both the student and their parents by providing academic, social, and emotional support. Because every situation is different and can change quickly, there is no one-size-fits-all approach. Ideally, an educational plan is designed early, adapts flexibly and is developed together with the hospital school, parents, student and support services. It remains relevant during absences, after the student’s return and often throughout the entire school journey. The plan should be reviewed regularly, both during treatment and after the return to school, so participation can be built up gradually or scaled back when needed.

The child’s regular school is not expected to design the educational care plan on its own. In most cases, the hospital school takes the lead in contacting the regular school (with parental consent), supported by the student guidance centre (CLB/CPMS), distance-learning organisations such as Bednet and ClassContact, and volunteer organisations like L’Ecole à l’Hôpital et à Domicile (EHD) and School & Ziekzijn (S&Z). In Flanders, schools can also provide lessons at home through the Temporary Home Education programme (TOAH).

Developing a plan usually involves:

  • Understanding the situation: medical factors, learning gaps, signs of distress, treatment schedules and any accommodations needed to support the student during absence and on return to school.
  • Setting educational, social, and wellbeing priorities, goals and expectations: choosing the most suitable educational format (or combination), prioritising subjects and competencies, agreeing on attendance frequency, finding ways to involve classmates in support and staying connected, and clarifying what is needed to progress to the next school year.
  • Approval and follow-up: approving the plan, coordinating across school staff, briefing classmates sensitively and adjusting through regular check-ins – especially towards the end of the school year to help the student succeed.
Part 1 › 4. Personalised educational care › Developing a plan

The regular school’s role: a shared responsibility

It reassured us that our child’s regular school remained ‘their school’. That sense of belonging was important, even when they couldn’t be there in person.

Celine – mother

Supporting a student affected by cancer is a shared responsibility that relies on collaboration between the regular school, the hospital school, home-education services, healthcare professionals and the family.

While these specialist services may temporarily take the lead during treatment, the regular school continues to play an essential role in maintaining the student’s sense of belonging, continuity and connection with everyday school life.

In practice, this role often includes:

  • Working with partners: cooperating with the hospital school, CLB/CPMS, Bednet/ClassContact, TOAH, and volunteer organisations like EHD and S&Z to shape the right educational mix and adapt as needed. Regardless of the chosen learning format, the student remains registered at their regular school.
  • Supporting the teacher(s), for example by:
    • appointing a central coordinator for structured follow-up
    • making clear agreements, together with support services, on reasonable learning goals, expectations, accommodations and differentiation strategies
    • recognising that social reintegration and wellbeing can be prioritised over performance at times
    • agreeing protocols for what can be shared with classmates (and their parents)
    • offering practical tools and guidance on what to say and do when welcoming a student back, preparing the class, dealing with peer dynamics and handling difficult situations (for example relapse or the student’s passing)
    • providing a ‘teaching partner’ for practical and emotional back-up
    • turning to partners such as the hospital school, the CLB/CPMS or the hospital psychologist for advice or a sounding board when staff are unsure how to handle a situation.

    All of this takes real time and energy, so it helps to consider how these tasks fit into teachers’ workload and how they can feel supported in their role.

  • Connecting the family and school community: serving as a bridge between the family, teachers and classmates, and helping to keep communication open.
  • Being responsive: noticing when extra help is needed and acting early.
  • Offering continuity: remaining a steady point of contact for the family, following up with the hospital school, gradually taking over again once the student starts returning part-time, and ensuring smooth information transfer to next-grade teachers or new schools.
Part 1 › 4. Personalised educational care › The regular school’s role: a shared responsibility

Learning away from school

Students with long-term illnesses have three official options for continuing their education while away from school:

  • The hospital school provides lessons in the hospital, coordinates with the regular school and with teaching at home, and helps prepare the return. Each hospital school provides its own brochure with practical information.
  • Live participation in class from a distance. Synchronous Online Learning (SIO) via Bednet/ClassContact facilitates live participation in lessons from home or hospital. The equipment and the service are free, for the family and for the school. Some students prefer fixed times and subjects; others connect flexibly when their energy allows. Many also enjoy joining breaks online, which can be just as valuable for maintaining friendships as the lessons themselves. Separately, some schools stream their own lessons through their usual platform, and some students prefer this.
  • A teacher at home (TOAH/volunteers) can be chosen when other options are not sufficient or not available. In Flanders, this is offered by ‘tijdelijk onderwijs aan huis’ (TOAH). Alongside this official initiative, volunteer organisations teach at home free of charge: School & Ziekzijn and Auxilia in Flanders, EHD and Auxilia in French-speaking Belgium.
Part 1 › 4. Personalised educational care › Learning from a distance

Staying in touch

We didn’t need perfect words – we needed steady ones.

Stephane – father

Staying connected with peers, receiving their support and feeling included is very important for a child or teenager with cancer. Friends can be a lifeline during illness – they lift mood, build confidence and help keep a sense of normality. Schools can play a key role in supporting this, ideally from day one. With the family’s and child’s permission, open communication with classmates and friends can help prevent misunderstandings, foster a supportive atmosphere, and ease reintegration when the student returns to school during or after treatment.

When following lessons is not possible, there are still many meaningful ways to stay connected:

  • Small and regular. Small, regular gestures – cards, drawings, notes, messages and brief online check-ins – can lift the student and reinforce their place in the group.
  • Timing and preferences. Check timing and preferences with the student’s parents, as energy levels can vary during treatment. Some students prefer written notes; others enjoy short video calls. When welcomed, a touch of humour can work wonders.
  • Involve the class. Try to involve the whole class (and friends in other classes) in brainstorming ideas and organising support, especially for older students.
  • School communication. Also make sure the student continues to receive routine school communications (newsletters, emails, key dates and assignments).
  • Help from other parents. Parents in the school community can also help – for example through meal schedules or transport rotations for siblings – particularly if the family has limited wider support. With the family’s consent, this can be coordinated informally or via the school’s parent association.

It was difficult for me to find my place again in my group of friends. I also had to rediscover myself, and felt very insecure.

Anke – student
Part 1 › 5. Classroom support › Staying in touch

Where to go next

Situation 03

How to welcome my student back to school?

Coming back to school is rarely a straight line. It brings joy, but also fatigue, worry and the fear of not fitting in – and there’s no fixed recipe. This part covers the practical adjustments to timetable and homework, how to prepare the class and your student before the return, and how to help classmates understand the exceptions.

Checklist

Before the return

  • The central coordinator contacts the family to understand the medical situation. Together, they update the educational care plan, agree on attendance and adjustments, and decide what may be shared with staff and classmates.
  • With the family’s consent, hold a brief class conversation to explain the adjustments needed, and agree on simple, low-pressure ways to welcome and support the student.

First weeks, and beyond

  • Check in regularly with the student and parents, monitor fatigue, learning and peer relations.
  • Record concerns, share them with the coordinator, the hospital school, and other support services (e.g. CLB/CPMS).
  • Review the educational care plan at set moments (e.g. once per term). Adjust workload/timetable where needed.
  • Ensure key information is passed on at transitions (new teachers, new school year).

What if my student is fading into the background?

  • Signal and share your concern. Note changes (withdrawal, silence, falling behind, absences) and share them with the central coordinator, school team and hospital school so you’re not carrying it alone.
  • Check in gently with the student and parents. Ask how school feels, what is hard, and what might help (socially and academically).
  • Review the educational care plan. See if expectations, workload, or timetable need adjusting so the student doesn’t withdraw because of fatigue or social concerns.
  • Strengthen peer understanding and inclusion. Use brief class conversations (with family’s consent) to explain adjustments, address jealousy/rumours, and invite simple support actions.
Annex 1 › Checklists › How to welcome the student back to school?

Learning at school

The standard school routine can be very demanding for children and teenagers affected by cancer, both during and after treatment. Returning to school, even part-time, is a major step. It can bring joy and excitement, but also worry, fatigue or fear of not fitting in any more. Although every return looks different, students often value the following.

Flexible timetables and attendance

  • Starting with shorter days or fewer subjects, then building up gradually – or scaling back again when needed
  • Adjusting physical activities when needed (e.g. because of fatigue or reduced immunity)
  • Having the option of a mix of school, home, hospital, or online learning as needed

Homework, assessments and progression

  • Flexible exam formats (e.g. extra time, oral exams, at-home tests or spreading out)
  • Clear and realistic expectations (e.g. lighter workloads, extra preparation time)
  • Early clarity on how progression will be handled. Within the possibilities of your school system, explaining clearly how decisions about moving up will be made can reduce a major source of stress. Many families say that knowing circumstances will be taken into account is a relief.

Connection and belonging

  • Being involved in decisions about learning, wellbeing and what is shared with peers
  • Feeling part of the group again without being labelled ‘the exception’
  • Not being excused too easily from tasks or activities; having alternative, meaningful ways to participate when full involvement is not possible
  • Classmates who understand adjustments and help with tasks (e.g. a buddy system)

Health and wellbeing

  • Small accommodations (e.g. permission to use cleaner staff toilets, mobility and writing aids such as laptops, quiet spaces, adapted classroom layouts, permission to wear hats or scarves)
  • Reassurance that health and wellbeing come first: permission to take breaks and practise self-care without guilt – pausing school is okay if health requires it
  • Encouragement and recognition of strengths to rebuild confidence
  • Respect for privacy and safety measures, which helps students settle back in
  • Infection prevention: coordinating with parents and the medical team, with an agreed system for notifying the family when a classmate falls ill.

Continuity in transitions

  • Returning to school without unnecessary extra formalities
  • Key information being passed on at year or school changes
  • Smooth handovers so that support continues without interruption

In short, the return to school is not only about education but also about regaining friendships and confidence. Supporting the student is not about following a fixed recipe, but about listening and adjusting to their evolving needs – academically, socially and emotionally.

Part 1 › 4. Personalised educational care › Learning at school

Welcoming the student back

I was afraid of saying the wrong thing, I didn’t know how to balance empathy and normality, and I worried it would be emotionally overwhelming without support.

Laurence – teacher

When a student is ready to return to school, it is common for teachers to feel a little worried about managing classmates’ and their own emotions. Many teachers find it helpful first to have a brief class conversation about any adjustments needed and to brainstorm simple ways to welcome the student back and offer support. The aim is not a perfect script or a ‘big fanfare’ welcome – most students prefer to blend in – but a calm, supportive atmosphere where they feel seen, respected, and included without extra pressure.

Part 1 › 5. Classroom support › Welcoming the student back

Coping with the exception regime

When special arrangements are made at school – extra time for tests, fewer tasks, the option to leave class early – families often worry about how classmates will react.

I was worried that the other kids would think my son was getting ‘VIP treatment’ or that he was lazy. In reality, every exception was something he needed but would rather not have.

Larissa – mother

Students themselves sometimes feel caught in the middle:

I felt so tired but also hated leaving class for a rest break. I could feel people looking at me and I didn’t know if they understood or thought I was just lucky.

Alexia – student

Many families say it helps when classmates – and their parents – understand why exceptions are needed, without going into private medical details. Simple explanations about tiredness, concentration, check-ups, or side-effects can reduce jealousy and rumours.

What helped me to feel less guilty was when the teacher said, ‘These adjustments are not rewards. They help things be fair – and fair doesn’t always mean “the same” – so he has the same chance as everyone else to keep up.’

Finn – student

I was relieved when the school sent a short message to other parents explaining that there were temporary adjustments so our child could keep up. This helped other parents reinforce the fairness framing and anticipate their child’s questions.

Catherine – mother

Even with explanations, frustrations can still pop up. Some teachers describe how helpful it was when there was space for classmates to express what felt strange or unfair – and then to end the conversation with a shared message of support and inclusion.

We talked together about what would make school feel safe and kind for everyone. Nobody was blamed, but it was clear that jokes, eye-rolling or comments about ‘favouritism’ were not okay.

Joke – teacher

A few students affected by cancer have also experienced teasing, exclusion or hurtful remarks, especially during breaks or online. They often say they wished adults had noticed early and checked in with them and the group, instead of waiting until it turned into bullying.

The best thing was when the teacher asked a small group of us how we could make things better for our friend, instead of just looking for who was guilty. That changed the atmosphere.

Elke – classmate

At the heart of these experiences is the same wish: that exceptions are seen not as special treatment, but as a way to keep the student connected, safe, and given a fair chance to succeed alongside their peers.

Part 1 › 5. Classroom support › Coping with the exception regime

Situation 04

Talking about cancer in class

Talking about cancer in class is one tool, not a requirement. Check first with your student and their family what feels right – sometimes small-group discussions or individual check-ins work better than a full class conversation. When you do talk, this part offers age-appropriate strategies, example phrases, activity ideas and educational resources.

Intro

When children or teenagers are confronted with cancer, an open and supportive environment can help them understand what is happening, express their feelings, and show empathy.

However, not every situation will require a big class conversation. Class discussions are one possible tool, not a requirement. Many students with cancer prefer to stay under the radar and do not want their illness discussed in detail. Before discussing cancer in class, it is therefore necessary to check what feels right with the student, their family, and, where relevant, the hospital team. In some cases, short discussions with small groups or individual check-ins work better than a full-class conversation.

When you agree together to involve the class, starting a conversation about cancer can feel challenging. You may worry about saying the wrong thing, sharing too much or too little, or protecting a student’s privacy while classmates look for information to offer meaningful support. Careful preparation can help you decide what questions you will and will not answer, how you will phrase things, and which information you can safely share. It can also be helpful to check whether any classmates have experienced cancer at home. A brief note to their parents can invite them to share any sensitivities you should be aware of.

Designed for teachers working with pre-schoolers, primary school children, or teenagers, this toolkit offers age-appropriate strategies, example phrases, activity ideas, and educational resources. It does not aim to make you a medical expert, but to help you feel less alone and better equipped when cancer becomes part of your school community.

Part 2 › 1. Intro
Checklist
  • You will need the family’s consent about what to share, when to talk, with whom, and how.
  • If the family agrees, you can prepare an age-appropriate explanation and hold a short class conversation. The hospital school or the hospital’s psycho-pedagogical team can help you with this, so don’t hesitate to contact them. Try to not overload students with medical detail, emphasise that their friend is still the same person but with temporary needs and limits, and explain that treatment may cause changes (tiredness, absences). Invite questions and correct rumours gently.
  • If you want to go further, you can prepare a lesson on cancer. This can help classmates better understand and cope with their friend’s illness. Ask permission from the family first.
Annex 1 › Checklists › What to say to my class?

Consent and privacy first

Consent from the student and family is always needed before sharing information about the student’s situation. Follow their lead and check in regularly, as their comfort level may change over time. Coordinate with the student and family on:

  • Purpose: discuss the benefits of class conversations and staying in touch.
  • Privacy and preferences: agree how to stay in touch, what to share, with whom, when and how.
  • Approach: agree in advance who leads class conversations (teacher, coordinator, student or parent, someone from the hospital team) and settle on tone, level of detail, and format. For example: a short update, a teacher-led question-and-answer session (with or without the student), or a testimony from the student (e.g. a vlog, letter or live presentation). An anonymous classroom notebox can be added to any of these, and often draws out what children are too embarrassed to ask aloud.
  • Siblings: discuss what can be shared with their class.
  • Other parents: agree on how to inform classmates’ parents before class conversations, to anticipate concerns or sensitivities.
  • School staff: agree on how to inform relevant school staff about class conversations or other actions, so they can answer questions sensitively.
  • Updates: ask whether the family would like feedback about how the conversations went.
Part 1 › 5. Classroom support › Consent and privacy first

Class conversations

No one told us anything – that’s when I got scared.

Amine – classmate

Classmates may struggle with their friend’s illness in different ways. Proactive, honest and age-appropriate class conversations can help inform peers, address concerns, prepare for changes and reduce anxiety, confusion, misinformation, excessive compassion, mockery and rumours. Regular check-ins also encourage empathy, so support grows more naturally. The suggestions in this section are meant to help you decide when to talk, what to cover and how to keep a steady, reassuring rhythm across the student’s journey.

Knowing how to help stopped me feeling lonely.

Billie – classmate
When to talk

Hold class conversations at least at two key moments: to announce the situation, and to prepare the class for the student’s return . Additional, regular check-ins during absence are recommended. On the day of return, you can also set up a short class conversation. However, most students dealing with cancer want their school experience to feel as normal as possible and rarely ask for an in-depth discussion about their illness.

Who can lead, and who can support
  • Class teacher (often preferred, especially with younger children): a familiar, trusted voice for age-appropriate framing. An unfamiliar adult in front of the class can raise anxiety rather than settle it.
  • Central coordinator, CLB/PMS coordinator or school psychologist: to support the teacher
  • Hospital psycho-pedagogical team: the psychologist can answer medical questions and address worries (with the child’s and parents’ agreement); the hospital-school teacher can explain how school at the hospital works
  • Student, siblings and/or parents: only if they express this wish and feel ready

In practice, the hospital team more often guides than leads: coaching the class teacher beforehand on difficult questions and emotions, or joining the conversation by video call when the class has many questions. A class visit in person is rarer, but this differs per hospital. Don’t hesitate to ask them early what’s possible.

How to talk

For practical guidance on talking about cancer in the classroom, . It covers the language and tone to use, how to involve classmates, how to support the ill student, how to follow up afterwards, and so on.

If things get tricky
  • Rumours. You might say, “Let’s pause and check the facts. Here’s what we do know.”
  • Jealousy about exceptions. You might say, “These are not privileges or rewards, and they’re not things your classmate wanted. They’re there so that someone who has missed a lot still gets a real chance to keep up. If you were in that situation, you’d get them too.”
  • Big questions (“Will they die?”). Acknowledge the feeling first, then answer honestly at an age-appropriate level. Something like: “Doctors have treatments that work, and they are doing everything they can to make [student name] better. Nobody can promise how it will go, and it’s okay to feel worried about that.” Always check with the parents, and where possible the hospital team, what can be said about this particular child before you find yourself answering. Offer one-to-one follow-up for children who seem especially worried.
  • Harassment or bullying. What helps are approaches that involve the whole group in building empathy and shared responsibility, rather than focusing on punishment.

Where to go next

Talking about cancer in class

General tips

This section offers general guidance for handling class conversations about cancer. If the student affected by cancer is present, there are a few extra points to keep in mind, which are noted where relevant.

Connect to your class conversation habits

No special rules are needed when talking about cancer. You can build on the way you normally organise a class discussion and name a few familiar reminders, for example:

  • We listen to each other without interrupting.
  • We do not mock or laugh at what others share.
  • If something feels uncomfortable, the teacher will help.

You can also think about the set-up of the conversation: will you sit in a circle or stay at desks; can students draw or fidget while listening; do some children prefer sitting a little further back? A cosy, predictable setting can make it easier for students to speak or simply listen.

Part 2 › 2. General tips › Connect to your class conversation habits

If the student is present

If the student affected by cancer is present, your role is to make sure they feel safe during the conversation. Avoid putting them in the spotlight, let them decide what they want to share, pay attention to how they respond to questions, and be ready to step in if they seem uncomfortable or upset. If they speak, a simple “thank you for sharing” is enough. Calling them brave may seem supportive (because they are), but it also underlines how hard the situation is, which may single them out. Teenagers especially value discretion and may prefer that only minimal information is shared about them. They are very aware of social dynamics and may worry about being seen as ‘the cancer patient’.

For guidance on communicating exceptions to classmates

Part 2 › 2. General tips › If the student is present

Your way of talking

Experience shows that these approaches often help:

  • Simple, concrete language. Use age-appropriate, relatable terms and avoid scary language or too many medical details.
  • Visual support. Drawings, simple diagrams, or story characters can help explain what is happening in the body. → Resources
  • Being honest but reassuring. Try not to minimise the seriousness of the situation, but avoid dramatic wording. Honesty builds trust and reduces confusion.
  • Focus on the present. Talk about what is known now rather than speculating about the future.
Part 2 › 2. General tips › Your way of talking

Involving and interacting with students

  • Invite questions. Make it clear that questions are welcome, during or after the conversation. If a question feels sensitive, you can help the student rephrase it. You will not have all the answers; it is fine to say you will check and come back to it later. If the student affected by cancer is present and wishes to speak, you can invite them to answer some questions. If not, explain that you will answer on their behalf. You can also set up a classroom notebox where children can post questions, feelings or concerns anonymously.
  • Check what they already know. From about six years onwards, you can ask what students have already heard about cancer or what they associate with the term. Some will have personal experiences. This can give you insight into their worries or assumptions. Consider having this check-in without the student affected by cancer. This gives you a chance to correct misconceptions (which can be hurtful), so the student can step in from a safer starting point.
  • Gently correct misconceptions. Children, especially younger ones, may worry about “catching” cancer or causing it. Offer reassurance and gently correct misconceptions such as “everyone who smokes gets cancer” or “cancer always means death”. What counts as reassuring depends a lot on age .
  • Notice and name emotions. Encourage classmates to express their concerns and feelings openly. They may feel sad, scared, angry, confused, guilty, curious, or nervous. Others may be eager to help. Finding words for their feelings can help them cope and develop empathy. Some children will have no particular feelings about the situation (or not yet), and this is also normal; a class conversation can invite reactions without expecting them. Not reacting outwardly does not mean a classmate does not care. You might say, for example: “People can have very different feelings about this, and some might not feel much at all. That’s okay too.”
  • Dealing with strong emotions. If a student reacts strongly (for example, refusing to see a classmate after an amputation), try not to dismiss their response. Instead, first try to understand what they are feeling. When they are ready, you can gently explain, for instance, that other family members were also worried at first, but then noticed that the scar wasn’t actually so scary.
Part 2 › 2. General tips › Involving and interacting with students

Creative activities

Discussing cancer in the classroom does not have to rely on talking alone. The document below brings together creative activities to explain cancer and explore emotions in a more engaging way, adapted for different ages.

Part 2 › 2. General tips › Creative activities

After the conversation

A single class discussion is rarely enough. In the days and weeks that follow, you can:

  • Keep an eye on students. Notice changes in behaviour, questions that arise in informal moments, or signs of worry.
  • Acknowledge feelings again. Briefly check how they experienced the conversation and remind them they can always talk to you individually.

If the student affected by cancer was present, it can be helpful to:

  • Check in privately. Ask how they felt during and after the conversation, and whether anything should be done differently next time.
  • Act early if issues arise. Respond quickly to any teasing or exclusion and, if needed, inform the central coordinator so you are not handling it alone.

Looking for more ways to keep the conversation going?

Part 2 › 2. General tips › After the conversation

Where to go next

Talking about cancer in class

Talking with different age groups

Children of different ages need different kinds of information and reassurance when talking about cancer. The points below can help you adapt your language and expectations. Whenever you use metaphors or materials, try to match what the family and care team are already using. Some hospitals, for instance, work with specific booklets or characters; using the same framework ensures your explanation doesn’t contradict what the ill student has been told at home or in hospital.

Pre-schoolers (ages 2.5–6)

Pre-schoolers live very much in the here and now. They are quickly saturated by explanations and usually need only short, simple messages and lots of reassurance.

How they understand illness
  • Illness is often seen as something temporary that “goes away”.
  • Magical thinking is common: they may believe that a thought or behaviour caused the illness.
How to talk
  • Keep it simple and concrete: “Your friend is very ill and needs to stay in the hospital for a while.” / “The doctors are giving strong medicine to help.”
  • Using stories and familiar metaphors can help them understand cancer in a way that feels safe.
  • Young children forget explanations easily, so gentle repetition helps.

Feelings and reactions
  • Emotions often come in short bursts and may be expressed more through play, behaviour or drawing than through long conversations.
  • Pre-schoolers may struggle with changes and a sense of insecurity. Reassure them that cancer is rare, nobody’s fault, not contagious and that doctors can often treat and cure it. For example:
    • “You cannot catch this illness like a cold. It’s safe to sit close, hug, or play together.”
    • “Nothing you did, said, or thought made your friend sick.”
    • “Sometimes your friend will be away or look different, but they are still the same friend.”
    • “Your classmate is bald now, but they can wear a cool hat.”
Support in class

While pre-schoolers can show empathy, they still see the world largely from their own perspective. Emphasise that children with cancer need love, friendship, and care. Simple actions can help them process feelings, develop empathy, and offer support: drawing a picture, singing a song or sending a card.

Part 2 › 3. Talking with different age groups › Pre-schoolers

Primary school children (ages 6–12)

Primary school children can handle basic explanations and are often curious, but they remain emotionally sensitive and need reassurance.

How they understand illness
  • Many are fascinated by the body and ask detailed questions.
  • They begin to understand that cancer is serious and that death is permanent.
  • Some want a lot of detail, others prefer to avoid the topic; both reactions are normal.
  • They often view connections in simple cause-and-effect terms, which can lead to misconceptions – for example believing that cancer is contagious or that everyone who smokes will get cancer.
How to talk
  • Offer a short, clear explanation of cancer, then let their questions guide the rest.
  • You can mention cells and treatments in simple terms, but there is no need to give a long science lesson when the conversation is about a specific classmate facing cancer.
  • A little more depth is possible if you are treating cancer as a general topic in the curriculum, or if the student with cancer explicitly wishes for a thematic lesson and the family agrees.

Feelings and reactions
  • From around age 8, children can better express their thoughts, but reflecting on their own emotions can still be difficult. They may worry silently about death, blame themselves or fear that other family members will get cancer.
  • Gently correct misconceptions, offer reassurance (as with younger children), and normalise emotions. For example: “Some of you might feel sad, worried or even cross – all of that is okay.”
Support in class

Younger primary school children (around ages 6–9) are often still quite egocentric, seeing things mainly in relation to themselves. They may not fully understand their classmate’s experience and might comment on physical changes or even tease them, especially if they do not understand what is happening.

Emphasise that children with cancer need love, friendship, and care. Encourage simple, concrete ways to be a good friend: saying hello, including the classmate in games when possible, sending messages or drawings — small, regular gestures that matter most .

Part 2 › 3. Talking with different age groups › Primary school children

Secondary school children (ages 12–18)

Teenagers can understand complex information but differ widely in how much they want to share.

How they understand illness
  • They grasp that cancer is serious and may follow stories in the media.
  • Some want detailed information about diagnosis, treatment and prognosis; others find this overwhelming.
How to talk
  • Start by checking what they already know and what they want to know.
  • Offer honest information in plain language, then stop before it becomes a lecture.
  • If you discuss types of cancer, treatments or innovative research, keep this general and curriculum-linked (for example in biology or ethics), rather than tying it closely to the student with cancer, unless they explicitly ask for this and the family agrees.
  • Listen more than you speak: invite questions or comments, but respect silence.

Feelings and reactions
  • Teens may feel sadness, fear, anger, or numbness, and may prefer to talk with peers rather than adults.
  • Acknowledge that it can be hard to know what to say to a friend with cancer and that awkwardness is normal. You might briefly share your own uncertainty (“I also sometimes don’t know what to say, but I’m here to listen”).
  • While they value independence, teenagers still look to adults for support and reassurance that cancer is rare, not contagious and often treatable.
Support in class
  • Emphasise small, everyday gestures over big projects: saying hi, including the classmate online or in group chats, keeping them updated on school life .
  • Some students facing cancer appreciate joint initiatives; others prefer that attention is not centred on them. Always check with the student and family first.
Part 2 › 3. Talking with different age groups › Secondary school children

Where to go next

Talking about cancer in class

Three conversations

There are three moments when a class conversation about cancer helps most. For each one, you’ll find its goals and a few phrases to get you started.

Announcing the situation

When: soon after the family gives consent to inform classmates

Main goals: reduce worry and confusion, set a caring norm, and brainstorm simple ways to stay connected

Possible elements:

  • Name the situation and reassure. “[Student’s name] has cancer. It’s a serious illness, but doctors are doing everything they can to help our classmate. We don’t really know why children get cancer, but we know that cancer isn’t contagious. You can’t catch it like a cold.”
  • Explain changes briefly. “They may be away from school for a while and might look different or be very tired because of the treatment.”
  • Normalise different reactions and invite questions. “People can feel sad, worried, curious, or not much at all – all of that is okay. You can ask questions now or later.”
  • Highlight simple support. “Small things matter: saying hello, sending a card or drawing, keeping them up to date with what happens in class.”

A short brainstorm on a few ways to stay in touch is often enough.

Part 2 › 4. Three conversations › Announcing the situation

Preparing the student’s return

Coming back was easier when my friends knew I might tire quickly.

Loriane – student

When: a few days or weeks before the student comes back, if the student and family agree.

Main goals: help classmates understand that return does not mean ‘everything back to normal’, prepare them for possible visible and invisible changes, and reduce jealousy or hurtful comments about adjustments.

Possible elements:

  • Explain the gradual nature of return. “Coming back to school is a big step, but it does not mean your classmate has fully recovered. It is not like flipping a switch, but a journey that takes time. They may still get tired quickly, have difficulty concentrating or need extra check-ups in hospital.”
  • Mention adjustments (and their reasons) briefly. “They might come for shorter days, skip some activities, or leave class to rest. These are supports they need, not special rewards.”
  • Emphasise continuity. “Even if some things have changed, they are still the same person who likes the same jokes, music, or games.”

You can end by agreeing on one or two concrete supports for the first days back, such as a buddy for transitions or someone who walks with them to the playground. Spread this role across a few students, because a single buddy can start to feel responsible for the returning student, which is too much to ask of a child. Rotating also avoids the buddy becoming isolated from their own friends.

Part 2 › 4. Three conversations › Preparing the student’s return

Involving the student

Most students dealing with cancer want their school experience to feel as normal as possible and rarely ask for an in-depth discussion about their illness. However, some appreciate a short, carefully prepared moment to say something themselves or to hear basic questions answered. Agree on this with the student beforehand.

When: usually shortly before or after return

Main goals: offer a gentle welcome, avoid putting the student on the spot, and clarify where questions can go.

Possible formats:

  • a brief teacher-led update with no questions
  • a few pre-agreed questions that the teacher answers (or answers together with the student if they choose)
  • a short message from the student (spoken, written or recorded), if they wish

Reassuring messages for the student:

  • “You only share what you want – I’ll take care of the rest.”
  • “If you do not feel like answering questions, classmates can ask me instead.”
  • “We’re glad you are here. Let’s think together about what will make school feel okay this week.”

Try to end the day with something light and ordinary – a game, a shared activity or simply spending time together – so the focus shifts from the illness to being back in the group.

Part 2 › 4. Three conversations › Involving the student

Where to go next

Talking about cancer in class

Finding the right words

What to say in the moment — a short guide for the primary years, and five ready-to-use scenarios for secondary school.

Primary school children (ages 6–12)

At this age, children may ask blunt questions (“Are you going to die?”), repeat things they’ve heard, or say something unintentionally hurtful. This is normal and not a sign of insensitivity, they are processing out loud.

Your role as a teacher is to guide these moments as they happen rather than trying to prepare children with conversation tips they cannot yet apply. A few things you can do:

  • When a child says something hurtful or inaccurate, correct gently and without drama. “That’s not quite how it works. Cancer isn’t something you catch from someone.”
  • When a child asks a difficult question, acknowledge it. “That’s a big question. Here’s what we know…” You don’t need to have all the answers.
  • Model the tone you want to see. If you’re calm, concrete, and kind, children will follow.

There are a few simple ideas children this age can grasp: that their classmate is still the same person, that including them matters, and that a drawing, a card, or saving a seat can mean a lot. Keep it concrete and action-based: what they can do, not what they should say.

Part 2 › 5. Finding the right words › Primary school children

Secondary school children (ages 12–18)

Just like adults, teenagers may worry about saying the wrong thing, which can lead them to avoid their friend altogether. You can help them connect more meaningfully by sharing tips from families who have experienced childhood cancer. We have translated their advice into five scenarios, which can be used as discussion prompts, a quiz, or short role-plays. You can read each scenario aloud, discuss it as a class, ask students what they would do, or invite volunteers to act out short responses – whatever suits your group best.

These scenarios may help classmates understand better what their friend is going through, and which words or actions are truly comforting. Pick whatever fits the class, skip the ones that don’t apply, or add new scenarios based on what you know about the group. They work best before or around the student’s return to school. If possible, do the activity without the student with cancer present, so classmates can speak freely.

Scenario 1: You don’t know what to say

Your classmate is back after months of treatment. You see them in the hallway. You want to say something but your mind goes blank, so you look away and walk past.

What could you do instead? Saying something small is always better than nothing. “Hey, good to see you” is enough. You don’t need the perfect sentence. If something comes out awkwardly, that’s fine too. Conversations always involve some trial and error. You can just say “maybe that came out wrong, but I’m glad you’re back.”

Scenario 2: The elephant in the room

You’re hanging out with your classmate and no one mentions cancer. It feels weird, like everyone is pretending nothing happened. But you also don’t want to make everything about their illness.

What works? You shouldn’t always wait for your classmate to bring up their cancer, because avoiding the topic can feel distancing or like you don’t care. But don’t make it the only subject either, because they probably miss normal chats about normal topics, jokes, and interests you share. School and friendships offer a sense of normality, which can be very comforting. So the key is to follow their lead: you can open the door, but they decide how far to walk through it.

Keep in mind that after everything your classmate has been through, some topics (such as celebrity gossip or small complaints) may feel less important to them, so be prepared that their interests may have shifted.

Scenario 3: They cancel on you, again

You’ve invited your classmate to hang out three times. They’ve said no every time, or cancelled at the last minute. You’re starting to think they don’t want to see you.

What’s probably going on? Treatment makes people exhausted, sometimes for days. They may want to come but simply can’t. The best thing you can do is keep inviting. You can also suggest alternatives, such as a shorter visit, an online call, or sending photos and updates. There’s no need for long messages: short, regular ones will already help them feel less isolated. And don’t take a slow reply or a last-minute cancellation personally, it almost certainly isn’t about you.

Scenario 4: They are upset and you want to help

Your classmate is having a bad day and starts crying. You feel you should say something encouraging like “Don’t worry, it’ll be okay” or “Try not to think about it” or “Stay strong, you’re a fighter, you’ll beat this!”

Why can that be tricky? The instinct to cheer someone up is natural and okay, of course. However sometimes, being overly positive can feel like their feelings are being brushed aside. You can encourage your friend, but you don’t need to “fix” their emotions. Let them express themselves freely, including crying, feeling angry or being quiet. Just being there and showing you care is one of the best things you can do.

What to say then? Something like “that sounds really hard” or “this really sucks and I’m here” is usually more honest and more comforting. It recognises what they’re going through without putting pressure on them to be brave or ‘win’ some kind of fight by trying harder. Whether cancer treatment works depends on medical factors, not on how ‘strong’ or ‘heroic’ someone is.

Scenario 5: You’re struggling too

Supporting a friend with cancer is hard. You feel sad, scared, or helpless, but you think you shouldn’t complain because they have it worse.

The truth is: your feelings matter too. You don’t have to be fine all the time. Talk to someone you trust, like your parents, a teacher, a friend. Looking after yourself isn’t selfish; it’s what helps you stay a good friend. And if you feel too upset to comfort them in person, that is okay. You can still show support with a small message that you are thinking of them.

Part 2 › 5. Finding the right words › Secondary school children

Situation 05

Supporting siblings

A cancer diagnosis also affects brothers and sisters. They may feel worried, overlooked, or burdened with new responsibilities at home. At school, this may show as concentration problems, fatigue, changes in behaviour, or absenteeism. Here’s how you can support them.

Voices from siblings

When my sister was in the hospital, I couldn’t concentrate. I was thinking about her all the time.

Louise – sister

Everyone asked about my sister, but nobody asked how I was doing.

Ada – sister

It feels like my schoolwork doesn’t matter anymore. I stopped trying as hard, but other times I push myself even more, so my parents don’t have to worry about me.

Thomas – brother

I was bullied because my sister didn’t have hair. It made me angry and sad.

Tille – sister
Part 1 › 4. Personalised educational care › Supporting siblings

What teachers sometimes notice:

A student who used to be lively suddenly became very quiet.

Elodie – teacher

We sometimes see siblings take on a lot of care responsibilities at home. At school, that can show up as tiredness or distraction.

Laurence – teacher

Siblings may feel invisible, which can make them act out in class. A simple chat can mean the world, while for others structural support may be necessary.

Zoé – teacher
Part 1 › 4. Personalised educational care › Supporting siblings

At school, siblings often appreciate

  • A trusted adult who is aware of the family situation, checks in gently and regularly, and keeps an eye on signs of distress
  • Being offered a say in whether their class is told anything at all, and if so what and when
  • Not being treated as the ‘messenger’ of updates
  • Understanding of changes in behaviour
  • Flexibility with workload and deadlines during stressful times
  • Understanding from classmates to prevent bullying or resentment
  • A teacher who keeps an eye on how they’re doing among classmates, and the choice to help share news with their class — or even lead that conversation themselves — if they wish and feel ready

Above all, siblings value school as a familiar place where they can spend time with peers and be themselves – not just ‘the sick child’s brother or sister’.

Where to go next

Situation 06 · here if you need it

When my student doesn’t get better

Sometimes, despite treatment, a child’s cancer turns out to be incurable. Schools then face the delicate task of supporting, where possible, the student, their family, and the wider school community through what comes next.

Checklist

When my student doesn’t get better

  • Don’t carry it alone. If you are the first one to know, share the news with the central coordinator / school principal and agree on the next steps.
  • Follow the family’s lead. Ask (via the coordinator) what they want the school to know and share. Don’t start conversations about prognosis unless clearly invited.
  • Understand the focus of palliative care, which is about quality of life and can last months or years, sometimes alongside continued schooling.
  • Keep school a place of normality and connection.
  • Support classmates gently, and share information only with the family’s permission.
  • Look after yourself too. It’s normal to feel overwhelmed; you can ask a colleague to join you for class conversations or rituals, and seek support from colleagues, CLB/CPMS, and the hospital or palliative care team.
Annex 1 › Checklists › When my student doesn’t get better

Understanding incurable cancer and palliative care

When doctors say a child’s cancer is incurable, it means that current treatments cannot make the cancer go away completely. This does not necessarily mean the child will die soon or that their quality of life cannot be good. Some children live with incurable cancer for months or even years, with treatment focused on slowing the disease, managing symptoms, and maintaining the best possible quality of life. This is what palliative care means: not the end of treatment, and not only the final weeks of life. The child’s cancer cannot be cured, but it can be managed.

During this time, many children still want to come to school, see their friends, and take part in everyday life as much as they can. School may become even more important as a place where they are still a student, not just a patient. Their energy and abilities may change from week to week, and plans may need to be adjusted at short notice. What matters most is that they feel welcome and included, without pressure.

It is normal to find this situation difficult as a teacher. You may feel helpless, sad, or unsure how to act around the child or their classmates. There are no perfect words or actions. Staying present, keeping things as normal as possible, and following the family’s lead will already make a difference.

Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › Understanding incurable cancer and palliative care

Respecting the family’s wishes

Talking about incurable cancer is very painful. Teenagers in particular often understand what is happening, and deliberately choose not to talk about their prognosis. It’s a way to protect themselves and their friends from further distress. For many, avoiding these conversations is a normal way of coping.

Many families say it helps when schools follow their lead. It is important to respect their wishes and to avoid initiating conversations about prognosis or end-of-life unless the family clearly invites this or asks for support.

Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › Respecting the family’s wishes

Creating a supportive environment

If the student is too unwell to attend school, you can still help them feel connected if the family wishes this. If they are still attending, the focus is often on safety, positivity and connection with peers.

  • Younger children. Offer a warm, reassuring environment. Join in with everyday activities and do not draw attention to the illness unless the child or family does.
  • Older students. Let them decide whether and when to talk about their condition. Many prefer simply being with friends and enjoying ordinary moments.

As the illness progresses, the student may no longer be able to come to school at all. Many schools hold back at this point, afraid of intruding on the family. But low-pressure gestures usually mean a great deal: a message that needs no reply, a card from the class, letting the family know their child is still being thought of. Make it easy to receive and easy to ignore – no questions to answer, no visit to arrange, no obligation to keep in touch. The message is that the school is still there, without expectations.

In all cases, it can help when teachers keep an eye on peer interactions, encourage kindness, and avoid talking about prognosis or death over the student’s head.

Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › Creating a supportive environment

When your student dies

Losing a student is one of the hardest things a school community faces. There is no way to prepare for the loss itself, but a school can help make the days that follow gentler, some of which is easier to arrange beforehand. Families often find comfort in knowing what the school will do, rather than facing those decisions in the days after their child dies. With the family’s permission, agree in advance how the school community will be informed and supported. Some schools open their doors during a weekend or holiday so classmates can come together and hold a ritual of their own (e.g. writing a letter, burning candles). The hospital’s psycho-pedagogical team can help with timing, wording, and supporting whoever delivers the news.

Contacting the family

The principal or central coordinator can contact the parents to ask how the school can help, how and when they would like the news to be shared, and whether they welcome a memorial or school involvement in the funeral.

Delivering the news
  • Decide who will deliver the news: often the class teacher, but sometimes the central coordinator or headteacher. It helps if the person is familiar to the students and supported by someone experienced, such as the hospital or school psychologist.
  • Share the news in small class groups rather than an all-school assembly.
  • Keep explanations clear, honest and compassionate without overwhelming students; the aim is to support grieving and strengthen community.
  • Watch for students who may need extra support, especially those who have experienced other forms of loss (e.g. a death in the family, a parent’s illness, or family separation).
Providing a script for teachers

A central coordinator or another staff member can take the initiative here, depending on what works best in your setting. Many teachers appreciate having a short script that can help them:

  • briefly explain what has happened
  • highlight positive memories or qualities of the student
  • outline how the school will honour the student
  • share practical funeral or condolence details (if the family agrees)
Supporting the person who shares the news

Whoever delivers the news should do so only if they feel able to. This person may need time and support themselves, and can be accompanied by a colleague. It can be healthy for children and young people to see adults expressing grief in an appropriate way.

Cultural and religious sensitivities

Customs around death and mourning vary across cultures and religions. Where relevant, find out what matters to the families and students involved, so that responses are respectful of their traditions.

Preventing rumours

Not everyone will hear the news at the same time, so you may need additional channels (letters or emails to parents, newsletters, staff meetings) to inform the school community and reduce confusion or rumours.

Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › When your student dies

Funeral and memorial ceremony

If the family agrees, classmates can be involved in the funeral or a memorial in simple, meaningful ways. They might bring flowers, drawings or a comforting object. Older students may read a poem, share memories or contribute to a collective artwork or memory project. The school can also organise its own memorial – for example a walk, a plaque, a tree or bench, a message book or an online remembrance page – in coordination with the family.

Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › Funeral and memorial ceremony

After the funeral

Grief continues well beyond the funeral. Schools can offer ongoing support to classmates and family by holding follow-up class conversations and keeping memories alive. This matters even more later on, when school life has found its rhythm again but the family is still deep in mourning. Small gestures can mean the world: a message on a birthday or an anniversary, an invitation to a school event, letting the family know their child is still remembered.

Later conversations in class ask for a different approach than the first ones. In the early weeks the class grieves together; months later, some children have moved on while others are still struggling. A conversation held for its own sake can leave the first group feeling insensitive and the second feeling out of step. It helps to anchor these moments to a specific occasion – a birthday, an anniversary, a milestone the student would have reached – and to offer writing alongside talking, so everyone can choose how much to contribute, or not to. Keep using the student’s name: when a name disappears, children often read it as a ‘ban’ on mentioning the student at all. Transitions deserve attention too, such as a new class group, a move to secondary school, or a teacher who never knew the student.

Gestures can also come years afterwards. One school invited a family to the graduation ceremony of the year their daughter would have finished school, three years after she died, and awarded an honorary diploma in her name. For the family, being remembered at the moment that would have been hers meant a great deal.

Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › After the funeral

Supporting grieving children

Grief looks different for everyone. Reactions vary by age, maturity, personality, and closeness to the person who has died – there is no single ‘right’ way to grieve. Bereaved children and grief professionals often highlight the following:

  • Consider age and understanding. Children’s grasp of death evolves with age and experience.
  • Recognise different coping styles. Some children talk, some stay quiet, others express emotions through play, behaviour, or creativity.
  • Do not underestimate the impact. Feelings may surface gradually, even if the child seems ‘fine’ at first.
  • Encourage questions and expression. Answer openly and simply, avoid confusing euphemisms (such as “gone to sleep” or “passed away”), and invite creative expression.
  • Do not avoid the subject. Silence can leave children alone with their worries.
  • Accept their grief. You do not need to ‘fix’ sadness. Avoid platitudes such as “be strong” or “time heals all wounds”. Acknowledge the loss and share memories.
  • Maintain routines with flexibility. Routines offer stability, but academic expectations may need adjusting.

For additional grief support

Annex 5 – Resources Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › Supporting grieving children

Keeping memories alive

One of the greatest fears for bereaved parents is that their child will be forgotten. Schools can help by keeping their memory present. Ways to honour the student include:

  • Including them in school traditions. For example, sending a card to the family on the child’s birthday, or creating an annual award in their name.
  • Encouraging personal tributes. Support classmates to share specific memories (“I’ll always remember how you…”) rather than general phrases like “We’ll miss you.”
  • Using symbolic gestures. With younger children, this could be a teddy bear in the class photo to represent their friend; with older students, a photo or a symbol can travel with the class from year to year. Whatever you choose, check with the parents and classmates first.

Parents who stay connected to the school often appreciate seeing that their child is still remembered. Whenever possible, let them see this in simple, heartfelt ways, and ensure all gestures are personal and meaningful – not just formal or ‘out of duty’.

Part 1 › 6. When your student doesn’t get better › Keeping memories alive

Situation 07

Where to go with my own questions and worries?

Supporting a student through cancer asks a lot of you too. You may worry about saying the wrong thing, or about how to balance empathy and normality. You don’t have to carry it alone, or have all the answers. Here’s who and what can help.

Support for teachers

I was afraid of saying the wrong thing, I didn’t know how to balance empathy and normality, and I worried it would be emotionally overwhelming without support.

Laurence – teacher
  • Hospital team: for tips, demos, and educational materials – also regarding siblings.
  • Colleagues, central coordinator, external coaches: when the class teacher feels uncomfortable or overloaded.
  • Guidance and resources: You can find tips, tools, and age-appropriate educational resources to talk about cancer in class here:

You can turn to:

  • Your central coordinator or school principal.
  • CLB/CPMS or other school counselling services.

Where to go next

Situation 08

Good to know – How does cancer affect your student?

School gives students with cancer more than learning: a welcome break from the medical world, a rhythm to the day, and a sense of belonging. Staying engaged helps them stay on track and rebuild confidence. It also makes coming back easier. But cancer and its treatment change what a school day asks of them. Concentration, energy, appearance, and friendships all shift — some effects are immediate, others last long after treatment ends.

Why school matters

Continuity, connection, and confidence

Schools play an important role in the lives of children and teenagers with cancer. They are a welcome distraction from the medical world, providing structure and a sense of normality. Beyond learning and reducing learning gaps, schools encourage social interaction, giving the student a sense of belonging, also during their absence. Staying engaged with school also shifts the focus to what the student can do, building confidence and offering perspective. For the ill student, school can be a reminder that life goes on and that the future is still theirs to shape. Ongoing involvement with school can also ease the return after treatment, both socially and academically, and supports the student in staying on track alongside their peers.

What school means however can differ from one student to another. Some value contact with classmates most, while others draw strength from continuing to learn. It is therefore worth exploring with the student what matters most to them.

Part 1 › 1. Why school matters

Difficulties

Understanding the cognitive, physical, and psychosocial impact of cancer.

Some students can attend school part-time during treatment; others only afterwards. In both cases, returning to school does not mean everything is back to normal. Recovery is always gradual, and challenges may continue for a long time. These differ widely depending on the student, type of cancer, and the treatment. Some difficulties appear straight away, others only emerge later, and some may become permanent.

"I used to finish tests quickly. After treatment, even reading the questions felt slow."

Lisa – student
Cognitive difficulties

Cancer treatments may affect work pace, concentration, memory, abstract thinking, staying organised, taking notes, and starting or finishing tasks. For students recovering from brain tumours in particular, cognitive and executive difficulties (e.g. planning, organising and focusing) can be long-lasting and may require ongoing support.

"Climbing the stairs to my classroom felt like running a marathon."

Suzan – student
Physical effects

School days are naturally structured around cognitive learning, so physical needs sometimes have to fit around the timetable. For example, toilet use may be limited to playtime for organisational reasons, rather than when the body needs it. For a student in treatment or recovery, managing physical needs in such a setting can be particularly challenging. Families often say they feel relieved when everyday routines can be adjusted a little to make things more manageable.

  • Fatigue. A whole school day or a busy classroom can be exhausting. Students may need shorter days, extra breaks, lighter timetables, or inclusive alternatives.
  • Reduced motor skills. Treatments can weaken muscles, bones, and joints, making even simple tasks like writing or carrying a bag harder. Some children need physiotherapy for years to rebuild strength.
  • Reduced immunity. Cancer and its treatment can weaken the immune system, making students more vulnerable to illness and infection, even after treatment has ended. The student's treating doctor will closely monitor their condition, evaluate how things are going at school, and determine when and under what conditions they can return.

"I looked fine on the outside, but inside I was still exhausted and anxious."

Bastien – student
Psychosocial impact
  • Visible changes. Treatments and medication may change appearance — for example hair loss, skin problems, or weight fluctuations — which can affect confidence or even trigger bullying.
  • Invisible struggles. Each student responds differently, but common challenges include fear of relapse, big life questions, separation anxiety, difficulty sharing attention in class, low self-esteem, mood swings, and behavioural changes such as anger outbursts or, conversely, withdrawal. Side effects of medication can intensify these issues.
  • Social hurdles. While some students reintegrate smoothly, others need more time and understanding to rebuild confidence and connections. They may struggle to reconnect with peers because of shifting friendships or new class groups. Changes in appearance, mood, and behaviour — together with school adjustments and limits on activities — can heighten feelings of isolation or difference. Expectations may also become too high when a student appears 'well' on the outside but is still struggling mentally. Classmates, too, may find it hard to know how to respond, which can sometimes lead to awkwardness, avoidance, jealousy, or even stigma.
Ups and downs

Cancer treatment often runs in cycles or phases, so side effects may be stronger one week and milder the next. The medical journey itself is also often unpredictable. A key challenge is therefore that the student’s physical condition can vary greatly. One week they can follow lessons; the next they cannot manage at all. Fatigue, headaches, nausea or concentration problems can make even short activities very difficult.
