Reference page

Questions and answers about cancer

This section brings together key questions about cancer, with answers for each age group.

Terms shown in green are glossary terms — click one to see its definition.

When using this Q&A in class, it can help to follow the questions’ order, as they build on each other. For example, you might start by explaining what cancer is, then reassure students that childhood cancer is rare, not contagious, and that doctors have effective treatments. This sequence can reduce misunderstandings and worries.

If the ill student is present during the conversation and agrees, you could go through some of the questions together beforehand and let them decide what they’d like to explain themselves. For some children, this can feel empowering, giving them a sense of agency and control over what is said, and offering a chance to share their perspective. It can also foster empathy and understanding among classmates.

Part 2 › 6. Questions and answers

Ages 2.5–6

What is cancer?

Our body is like a busy city made of tiny bricks (cells). Workers are always building new walls and repairing old ones. Almost always the bricks are strong and everything works. But sometimes a brick breaks on its own. The workers do not notice, so they keep building with it, and the broken bricks pile up into messy buildings (tumours) in places where they do not belong. Those buildings get in the way, and some of them can even block the roads, so the city cannot work properly. This is what happens with cancer.

How does someone get cancer?

The workers in our body usually do a great job. Sometimes, a brick breaks. We do not know for sure why, but it is nobody’s fault. Not yours, not your friend’s, not anyone’s. Luckily, this rarely happens to children.

Is cancer contagious?

Cancer is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else like a cold or the flu. This means you can sit next to, hug, play with, and talk to someone who has cancer without any risk. It is completely safe.

How do doctors find out if someone has cancer?

Doctors usually start looking when someone doesn’t feel well for a long time, or has a visible lump. They use special tests to find out what is wrong. These tests help doctors see whether there are broken bricks (cancer cells), where they are, and how best to clear them away.

How do doctors cure cancer? Can someone get better?

Getting better from cancer is not like getting better from a cold. It’s not like taking one pill and being fine the next day. It takes a long time, with many visits to the hospital. Doctors choose what works best for each child. They can take out the broken bricks, use strong medicines to get rid of them, or help the body fix things by itself. The good news is that many children do get better and can go back to doing what they love.

Does cancer hurt?

When you have the flu, medicines usually make you feel better quickly. With cancer, it’s different. Cancer medicines are very strong. Because of that, children with cancer often feel worse first, and only better later. That’s normal. The medicines can make them tired or give them a tummy ache, and sometimes their hair falls out. Cancer itself doesn’t always hurt, but the medicines sometimes do. Luckily, doctors have other medicines that make the pain less. When the treatment stops, most children slowly start to feel better again.

How does cancer make someone feel?

Having cancer can make someone feel sad, scared, angry, exhausted – and sometimes very lonely. If you know someone with cancer, you can help by being kind, playing with them, or giving them a big smile and a gentle hug. Just being a good friend can help them feel happy and loved.

Part 2 › 6. Questions and answers › Ages 2.5–6

Ages 6–12

What is cancer?

Cancer is a disease of the cells. Healthy cells can split into two new cells when the body needs them, and then they stop dividing again. With cancer, that brake no longer works: the cells divide too fast and don’t stop when they should. The new cells that are made behave in the same way and don’t stop dividing either. This leads to far too many abnormal cells in the body.

Over time, these abnormal cells can:

  • either form a lump (called a tumour), or pile up in the blood
  • invade the tissue around the lump, damage healthy cells and take up a lot of space, so the body can no longer work properly
  • break away from the original lump, travel to other parts of the body and form new lumps there (but this doesn’t always happen)

Because cells are everywhere in the body, cancer can start almost anywhere.

How does someone get cancer?

As our bodies grow and change, small mistakes can sometimes happen by chance. These mistakes usually do no harm and the body usually repairs them, but sometimes they can lead to cancer. Luckily, this is very rare in children. Most young people will never get cancer. Why do these mistakes happen? In adults, cancer is sometimes caused by pollution or unhealthy habits like smoking or drinking alcohol, but in children this is almost never the case. The truth is, no one knows exactly why some children get cancer. The most important thing to remember is: cancer is nobody’s fault.

Is cancer contagious?

Cancer is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else like a cold or the flu. This means you can sit next to, hug, play with, and talk to someone who has cancer without any risk. It is completely safe.

On the other hand, during treatment your classmate can get sick more easily from your cold. That’s why it’s a good idea to wash your hands regularly, especially when you’re feeling ill yourself.

How do doctors find out if someone has cancer?

Doctors usually start looking when someone doesn’t feel well for a long time, or has a visible lump. The signs of cancer (symptoms) can be different depending on where it begins in the body. Doctors use special tests to find out what is wrong. These tests help them see whether there are cancer cells, where they are, and which treatment might work best.

Common tests include:

  • Blood tests: a small sample of blood is checked for signs that something is wrong.
  • Biopsy: a small piece of a lump or tumour is taken and examined under a microscope to see if it is benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer).
  • X-rays: pictures of hard tissues like bones to look for unusual changes.
  • MRI scans: detailed pictures of soft tissues like muscles, organs, and the brain.
  • PET scans: a special liquid helps light up cancer cells in pictures.

How do doctors cure cancer? Can someone get better?

The positive news is that childhood cancers can often be treated successfully. Doctors choose a treatment based on the type of cancer, where it is, how advanced it is (the stage), and the child’s overall health. Sometimes doctors combine treatments to increase the chance that all cancer cells disappear.

The main treatments are:

  • Surgery: an operation to remove the tumour
  • Chemotherapy: medicines that destroy cancer cells
  • Radiotherapy: high-energy rays that target and damage cancer cells
  • Immunotherapy: helps the immune system recognise and attack cancer cells
  • Targeted therapy: drugs that target cancer cells while aiming to spare healthy cells

Treating cancer is hard and can take months or even years. Some cancers are still difficult to treat, but new therapies are helping more children recover. Even after treatment ends, regular check-ups continue.

Does cancer hurt?

Cancer itself doesn’t always hurt, but the treatments sometimes do. Many people expect someone with cancer to feel better straight away once treatment starts, but at first it’s often the opposite. Because of the medicines, people often feel worse before they feel better, and that’s completely normal. The medicines are so strong that they don’t only affect cancer cells, but sometimes healthy cells too. This causes side effects, which can make someone feel unwell.

Common side effects:

  • tiredness (fatigue)
  • feeling sick (nausea)
  • hair loss
  • changes in appetite or weight
  • skin changes
  • a weaker immune system
  • emotional ups and downs

Some days may feel better than others. Having bad days does not automatically mean the cancer is getting worse – it is often a result of the treatment being so strong. Once treatment is over, most people start to feel better again. If a patient has pain, doctors can prescribe medicines to ease it.

How does cancer make someone feel?

Having cancer is really tough. It is normal to feel sad, scared, angry, exhausted, lonely, or frustrated at times – especially when someone cannot do everything they used to do. If you know someone with cancer, you can help by being kind, spending time with them, and letting them know you are there if they want to talk. Even small acts of kindness – a message, a joke, or simply sitting with them – can make a big difference. Support from family, friends, doctors and nurses helps them feel cared for and less alone.

Part 2 › 6. Questions and answers › Ages 6–12

Ages 12–18

What is cancer?

Cancer is a disease of the cells. It happens when some cells stop working properly. Healthy cells can split into two new cells when the body needs them, and then they stop dividing again. With cancer, that brake stops working: the cells divide too fast and don’t stop when they should. This happens because mistakes (mutations) have crept into the cell’s DNA by chance, or because genes are switched on or off in the wrong way. The new cells behave in the same way, which leads to far too many abnormal cells in the body.

Over time, these abnormal cells can:

  • either form a lump (called a tumour), or build up in the blood.
  • invade the tissue around the tumour, damaging healthy cells so the body no longer works properly.
  • break away from the original tumour, travel elsewhere, and form new tumours. This spreading (metastasis) makes cancer harder to treat, but it doesn’t happen to everyone.

A tumour that invades and damages surrounding tissue is called malignant, or cancer. Because there are cells everywhere in the body, cancer can start almost anywhere.

What types of cancer affect children?

Childhood cancer is complex and diverse, with many different types. These are often grouped into two main categories:

  • Solid cancers: cancer cells form lumps or tumours in one part of the body. These can grow and invade nearby tissues and sometimes spread to other parts of the body (secondary cancers or metastases).
  • Liquid cancers: cancer cells circulate freely in the blood and bone marrow rather than forming a solid lump.

The specific type of cancer is usually named after the kind of cells or tissue where it starts. Examples include:

  • Leukaemia: cancer of blood-forming cells (liquid),
  • Brain and spinal cord tumours: cancers of the central nervous system (solid),
  • Neuroblastoma: cancer of certain nerve cells (solid),
  • Lymphoma: cancer of the lymphatic system (liquid, but often forms lumps in the lymph nodes),
  • Sarcoma: cancer of bones, muscles or other connective tissues (solid).

Each of these types also has several subtypes; there are, for example, different forms of leukaemia. Some childhood cancers share names with adult cancers, but they are often biologically different and need different treatments.

How does someone get cancer?

As our bodies grow and change, small mistakes can sometimes happen in our cells by chance. These mistakes usually do no harm, and repair themselves, but sometimes they lead to cancer. Luckily, this is very rare in children and teenagers. Most young people will never get cancer.

Why do these mistakes happen? The truth is, no one knows exactly why some children get cancer. Nothing anyone did, or failed to do, caused it. The most important thing to remember is: it is nobody’s fault.

As people grow older, some things can raise the risk of developing cancer – habits like smoking or too much sun, but also things that are harder to control, such as pollution and genetics. In rare cases, a change in DNA (a mutation) is inherited from a parent, making someone slightly more likely to develop cancer than average. That doesn’t mean they will. Not all cancers can be prevented, but healthy choices help reduce the risk in later life.

Is cancer contagious?

Cancer is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else like a cold or the flu. Colds and flu spread through germs when someone coughs, sneezes, or shares food or drinks. Cancer works differently. It develops because of changes in cells inside the body, not because of germs that pass from person to person. This means you can sit next to, hug, play with, and talk to someone who has cancer without any risk. It is completely safe.

On the other hand, during treatment your classmate can get sick more easily from your cold. That’s why it’s a good idea to wash your hands and keep a little distance when you’re ill yourself.

How do doctors find out if someone has cancer?

Doctors usually start looking when someone doesn’t feel well for a longer period, or has a visible lump. The signs of cancer (symptoms) can be different depending on where it begins in the body. Doctors use special tests to find out what is wrong. These tests help them see whether there are cancer cells, where they are, and which treatment might work best.

Common tests include:

  • Blood tests: a small sample of blood is checked for signs that something is wrong.
  • Biopsy: a small piece of a lump or tumour is taken and examined under a microscope to see if it is benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer).
  • X-rays: pictures of hard tissues like bones to look for unusual changes.
  • MRI scans: detailed pictures of soft tissues like muscles, organs, and the brain.
  • PET scans: a special liquid helps light up cancer cells in pictures.

How do doctors cure cancer? Can someone get better?

The positive news is that childhood cancers can often be treated successfully, and they tend to respond better to therapy than many adult cancers. Doctors choose a treatment based on the type of cancer, where it is, how advanced it is (the stage), and the child’s overall health. Sometimes doctors combine treatments to increase the chance that all cancer cells are destroyed.

The main treatments are:

  • Surgery: an operation to remove the tumour
  • Chemotherapy: medicines that destroy cancer cells
  • Radiotherapy: high-energy rays that target and damage cancer cells
  • Immunotherapy: helps the immune system recognise and attack cancer cells
  • Targeted therapy: drugs that target cancer cells while aiming to spare healthy cells

Treating cancer can be challenging and may take months or even years. Some cancers are still difficult to treat, but new therapies are helping more children and teenagers recover. When there are no more visible signs of cancer, this is called remission. If someone stays cancer-free for more than five years, doctors usually consider them cured.

More than 80% of children with cancer in Belgium now survive, but some have side effects that appear only later, such as growth delays or learning difficulties. Even after treatment ends, regular check-ups continue. Some receive maintenance therapy to help stop the cancer coming back. If it does return, this is called a recurrence or relapse.

Does cancer hurt?

Cancer itself doesn’t always hurt, but the treatments sometimes do. Many people expect someone with cancer to feel better straight away once treatment starts, but at first it’s often the opposite. Because of the medicines, people often feel worse before they feel better, and that’s completely normal. The medicines are so strong that they don’t only affect cancer cells, but sometimes healthy cells too. This causes side effects, which can make someone feel unwell.

Common side effects:

  • tiredness (fatigue)
  • feeling sick (nausea)
  • hair loss
  • changes in appetite or weight
  • skin changes
  • a weaker immune system
  • emotional ups and downs

Some days may feel better than others. Having bad days does not automatically mean the cancer is getting worse – it is often a result of the intense treatment. Once treatment is over, most people start to feel better again. If they have pain, doctors can prescribe medicines to ease it.

How does cancer make someone feel?

Having cancer can be really tough. It is normal to feel sad, scared, angry, exhausted, lonely, or frustrated at times – especially when someone cannot do everything they used to do.

If you know someone with cancer, you can help by being kind, spending time with them, and letting them know you are there if they want to talk. Even small acts of kindness – a message, a joke, or simply sitting with them – can make a big difference. Support from family, friends, and medical professionals helps them feel cared for and less alone.

Why is research important?

Scientists work every day to study cancer and to develop better treatments that help people recover more often, more quickly, and with fewer side effects. Thanks to research, survival rates have improved and many families have more hope.

However, research into childhood and adolescent cancers is still underfunded compared with research into adult cancers. More funding is needed to develop safer treatments and support long-term survivors. Organisations like KickCancer raise money to help scientists make progress, so that young patients can live full and healthy lives.

Glossary

The glossary below can help you define and explain common cancer-related words. For each word, there is a simple definition suitable for younger children (ages 3–8) and one for older children, teenagers, and adults.

Annex 4 › Glossary

B

Benign
Ages 2.5–8

Not cancer. A lump in the body that is not dangerous.

Older

Benign cells are not cancer. They divide more than they should and pile up, but they don’t spread to other parts of the body. A benign tumour is usually a harmless lump of cells that can often be removed with surgery. Sometimes benign cells can become cancerous, so doctors keep a close eye on them.

Biopsy
Ages 2.5–8

When the doctor checks a tiny piece of the body to see if it is healthy or not.

Older

A test to diagnose cancer. The doctor takes a tiny piece of tissue from a lump (tumour) and examines it under a microscope to check whether the cells are malignant (cancer) or benign.

Blood cells
Ages 2.5–8

Tiny helpers in the blood that help us run, play, and grow.

Older

Our blood contains three types of blood cells: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells carry oxygen from our lungs to other body parts. They also take carbon dioxide back to the lungs, where we breathe it out. White blood cells help fight infections. Platelets are like plasters — when you get a cut, they help stop the bleeding by making a little plug.

Bone marrow
Ages 2.5–8

Jelly inside bones that makes blood cells: a little blood factory!

Older

Soft, spongy material inside bones that makes red and white blood cells, and platelets.

Annex 4 › Glossary

C

Cancer
Ages 2.5–8

A disease in which broken cells pile up and get in the way of the healthy cells.

Older

Cancer is the name for more than 200 diseases of the cells. Abnormal cells grow and divide too rapidly and in an uncontrolled way. Cancer cells don't work properly due to random mistakes (mutations) in their genes (DNA). They form a lump (tumour) or pile up in the blood, harm normal cells (making it harder for the body to work properly), and may spread to other parts of the body (metastasis), making cancer even more difficult to control.

Cell division
Ages 2.5–8

Some cells have a special talent. They can split to make two new cells which replace old or damaged cells.

Older

Cells grow, divide, and multiply to replace old or damaged ones. Some divide often (like skin and blood cells), others rarely divide (like brain and heart muscle cells). If the latter are damaged, they often cannot be repaired or replaced.

Cells
Ages 2.5–8

Tiny parts that make up our body. Each cell has its own job, so the body works well and stays healthy.

Older

Humans are made up of trillions of cells, the basic building blocks of life. About 100 cells fit inside a printed dot, so you need a microscope to see them. Each cell is like a tiny factory with a specific role, defined by which parts of its DNA are switched on. Muscle cells help us move, lung cells are for breathing, and stomach cells help to digest food. Unlike building blocks, cells are alive. They are born, grow, do their job, and eventually die. When a cell dies, a new one often takes its place, like swapping a puzzle piece to keep the whole picture complete.

Chemotherapy (chemo)
Ages 2.5–8

Special medicines that clear away the cancer cells.

Older

A cancer treatment that uses strong medicines to destroy cancer cells, or at least stop or slow their growth and division. Chemo often also affects healthy cells, which can make the patient feel tired or sick. These are called side effects.

CT scan
Ages 2.5–8

A way of using invisible light to take pictures of the inside of the body, to check if something is wrong.

Older

A scan that uses X-rays, a kind of invisible super-light that lets doctors look right through the body. Unlike a regular X-ray, the machine takes pictures of the body in thin slices. This shows whether cancer is present and exactly where it is. CT stands for ‘computerised tomography’.

Annex 4 › Glossary

D

Diagnosis
Ages 2.5–8

When the doctor works out what is making someone sick.

Older

Working out what kind of disease someone has by examining the symptoms and test results.

DNA
Ages 2.5–8

A tiny recipe book inside every cell. It tells the cell how to grow, work, and divide.

Older

Each cell contains DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), a large molecule that carries all its genetic information. Think of DNA as a recipe book with instructions that tell cells how to function, grow, and divide — and when to stop. All living things, from bacteria and plants to animals and humans, need DNA to survive.

Annex 4 › Glossary

I

Immune system
Ages 2.5–8

The body’s guards. They protect us from tiny bugs (germs) that can make us sick. Sometimes the guards need help from medicines, but most of the time they’re strong enough to keep us healthy.

Older

Different parts of the body working together to protect us against harmful invaders such as bacteria, viruses, and other germs. White blood cells play a key role: they track down invaders, destroy them and often even remember what they look like, so they can defend the body even better and faster next time. Our immune system is always working in the background to keep us healthy.

Immunocompromised
Ages 2.5–8

When someone gets sick very easily.

Older

A state in which the immune system is weakened, often caused by disease or treatment. Someone who is immunocompromised needs to be extra careful and avoid contact with anyone who is ill, even with something as minor as a cold.

Immunotherapy
Ages 2.5–8

Medicines that help the body’s guards recognise and clear away cancer cells.

Older

A cancer treatment that trains the patient’s own immune system to recognise and attack cancer cells faster and more effectively.

Annex 4 › Glossary

L

Lymph nodes
Ages 2.5–8

Little nets that catch and clear away tiny bugs (germs). When someone is ill, these sometimes get bigger. That means the nets are working hard to protect the body.

Older

Small, bean-shaped glands that are part of the immune system. They act like filters to trap and remove germs, waste, and harmful substances.

Lymphatic system
Ages 2.5–8

A cleaning crew in the body that works together with the guards. It keeps us healthy by catching tiny bugs (germs) and carrying them away.

Older

Part of the body’s immune system. It moves a special fluid, called lymph, around that helps the body get rid of germs and waste, keeping us healthy.

Annex 4 › Glossary

M

Maintenance therapy
Ages 2.5–8

When someone is given medicine for a long time to help keep the cancer away.

Older

A lighter treatment given for months or years after the main treatment (like chemo or radiation) is done. It is given to help clear any remaining cancer cells and lower the chance of the cancer coming back.

Malignant
Ages 2.5–8

Another word for cancer. The opposite of benign.

Older

Cells in malignant tumours divide rapidly, without control. They often invade nearby tissues and can spread to other parts of the body. Cancer cells damage normal cells, making it hard for the body to function properly.

Metastasis
Ages 2.5–8

When the cancer cells have travelled to another part of the body.

Older

Normal cells stay where they belong, but cancer cells break all the rules. Metastasis happens when cancer cells spread from one part of the body to another. They escape from the first tumour (primary tumour), travel through the blood or lymph fluid, settle in new areas and continue dividing there, sometimes growing into a new tumour (secondary tumour). Metastasis makes cancer treatment more difficult, but doctors do everything they can to stop these travelling cancer cells.

MRI scan
Ages 2.5–8

A way of using a big magnet to take pictures of the inside of the body, to check if something is wrong.

Older

A large machine used to detect cancer. Its magnets and radio waves create detailed, cross-sectional images of soft tissues, like muscles, organs, and the brain. The person lies on a bed that slides into a tunnel while the machine takes pictures. MRI stands for "magnetic resonance imaging".

Mutation
Ages 2.5–8

A tiny mistake in how the body is built.

Older

A change in DNA instructions that can make cells act in the wrong way. Mutations happen by accident when cells divide. In adults, mutations can also be caused by unhealthy factors like pollution or smoking, but childhood cancers are almost never linked to these. Our bodies are really good at fixing these mistakes, but if a mutation is not repaired, it can lead to cancer.

Annex 4 › Glossary

O

Organ
Ages 2.5–8

A part of the body, like the heart, lungs, or stomach.

Older

A part of the body made from tissues that do a job, like breathing, pumping blood, or digesting food.

Annex 4 › Glossary

P

Palliative care
Ages 2.5–8

When a special team of helpers (doctors, nurses, etc.) gives medicines or other care to make someone feel as good as possible, taking away pain or worries.

Older

Care for people with an illness they could die from, such as cancer. Palliative care doesn’t cure the illness, but it eases symptoms of the illness and side effects of treatment, such as pain and nausea. The aim is to help someone live as well as possible, even while they are ill, by caring for both body and mind. Ideally, this care starts as soon as treatment begins. So receiving palliative care doesn’t mean someone will die: recovery is still possible. It can last as long as needed, for months or years, with better and worse periods. Children receiving palliative care can still go to school, full-time, part-time or for short visits. End-of-life care is a special form of palliative care. It only starts when treatments no longer work and the doctors expect that someone is in the last phase of life.

Port-a-cath
Ages 2.5–8

A small button under the skin that lets doctors give medicines and take blood without having to use lots of needles. It stays there for as long as the treatment lasts, which is usually many months.

Older

A small device placed under the skin, usually on the chest, and connected to a large vein. Doctors and nurses use it to give chemotherapy, other medicines and fluids, and to take blood samples, without having to find a new vein each time. It stays in place throughout treatment, often for many months. Once treatment is finished, the port-a-cath is removed in a minor procedure.

PET scan
Ages 2.5–8

A way of taking pictures of the inside of the body in which cancer cells light up.

Older

A medical test used to detect cancer. The patient is given a small, safe dose of radioactive liquid. Cancer cells absorb more of this liquid than healthy cells, which makes them light up like little lamps. This helps doctors find hidden cancer cells. PET stands for ‘positron emission tomography’.

Annex 4 › Glossary

R

Radiotherapy / Radiation therapy
Ages 2.5–8

Strong, invisible beams that shrink or kill cancer cells.

Older

A precise cancer treatment using high-energy radiation to shrink, damage or destroy cancer cells so they cannot grow, multiply, or spread. The beams are aimed carefully at the tumour, keeping the healthy tissue around it as safe as possible. They are painless, though side effects such as tiredness or skin irritation may occur.

Recurrence / Relapse
Ages 2.5–8

When cancer comes back after getting better.

Older

When cancer returns after a period of remission.

Remission
Ages 2.5–8

When cancer goes away after treatment.

Older

When cancer cells and symptoms reduce or disappear thanks to treatment. Cancer is under control but may not be gone forever, so doctors need to keep checking it.

Annex 4 › Glossary

S

Side effects
Ages 2.5–8

When feeling sick or tired because of medicines. Most go away after some time.

Older

The unwanted effects of treatment. Some effects happen right away (nausea, fatigue, hair loss, changes in appetite, skin changes, mouth sores, weakened immune system, and emotional changes), while others may appear months or even years later, especially in young patients. Late effects can include growth problems, heart issues, or learning difficulties. Side effects occur because cancer treatments can damage healthy cells as well as cancer cells. The healthy cells usually recover after a while (e.g. hair grows back), so most side effects go away and doctors work hard to prevent or relieve them.

Solid / Liquid cancers
Ages 2.5–8

Solid means cancer cells form a lump, liquid means they move around the body.

Older

There are two main categories of cancer. In solid cancers, cells form a tumour in one place. They grow uncontrollably due to rapid cell division and invade nearby tissues, causing harm. Solid cancers can spread to other parts of the body over time, and may create secondary cancers. Liquid cancers mostly don’t form lumps (except for lymphomas) but move around through the blood or lymphatic system. They affect the bone marrow, blood, and lymph nodes.

Stage
Ages 2.5–8

Tells how far the cancer has grown or spread.

Older

Describes how far the cancer has grown or spread. This is needed to choose the appropriate treatment. The stage of cancer depends on its type, the size of the tumour (small like a marble or large like an orange), and location (in one place or spread). It usually ranges from 1 to 4. Stage 1 means the cancer is small and has not spread; stage 4 means it has spread to other parts of the body (metastasis).

Surgery
Ages 2.5–8

When the doctor takes out the lump during an operation.

Older

A cancer treatment where a surgeon removes the tumour during an operation. Surgeons try to remove the whole tumour, but some cancer cells may remain, so other treatments like chemotherapy or radiotherapy are often needed after surgery.

Symptoms
Ages 2.5–8

Something you feel or see when you're not well.

Older

Changes caused by an illness. People can feel (e.g. sore, itchy) or see (e.g. redness, a lump) these changes when something's not right in the body. Symptoms help doctors work out what is wrong.

Annex 4 › Glossary

T

Targeted therapy
Ages 2.5–8

Special medicines that mostly target cancer cells and try to spare healthy ones.

Older

A precise cancer treatment that works like a key fitting a specific lock. It identifies and attacks cancer cells while largely sparing healthy ones, which reduces side effects.

Tissue
Ages 2.5–8

A group of cells that work together.

Older

Groups of similar cells working together to do a job, like muscle, skin, or brain tissue.

Treatment / Therapy
Ages 2.5–8

What doctors do to help someone get better.

Older

Ways to treat cancer, like surgery (removes the tumour from the body), chemotherapy (strong medicines that destroy cancer cells), radiation (powerful beams that destroy cancer cells), immunotherapy (helps the immune system fight cancer), or targeted therapy (attacks only cancer cells).

Tumour
Ages 2.5–8

A lump in the body that shouldn't be there.

Older

When cells divide too much, they can pile up and form a lump. Early lumps of cells are often harmless, and sometimes even destroyed by the immune system. When the lump keeps on growing it is called a tumour. Not all tumours are cancer. For example, a mole on your skin is a small benign tumour of pigment cells. The word tumour simply means a lump of cells; it does not indicate whether the lump is benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer). Only solid cancers form tumours, liquid cancers don’t.

Annex 4 › Glossary

X

X-rays
Ages 2.5–8

A picture of the inside of the body that shows the bones especially well.

Older

A machine used to detect cancer. It takes pictures of hard tissues like bones and teeth by sending invisible, high-energy rays through the body. They can spot broken bones or tumours.
